title: Frankly Speaking, Frank Smith Is Wrong to Treat Reading as a Biologically Primary Skill
author: Harriett Janetos
summary: Harriett Janetos examines Frank Smith's foundational claim in Understanding Reading -- that reading is as natural as spoken language and can be learned by children in the same self-directed way they learn to talk -- and argues that this is a category error that produced cascading damage through the whole-language movement. The critique rests on David Geary's distinction between biologically primary skills (acquired implicitly through immersive experience, like speaking) and biologically secondary skills (acquired slowly through explicit instruction, like reading) -- a distinction Smith never acknowledges. Using Stanislas Dehaene's neuroscience on how the brain processes print differently from speech, Janetos argues that alphabetic print is a cultural invention requiring explicit teaching of grapheme-phoneme correspondences to create the neural connections fluent reading requires. The practical consequence of Smith's misclassification: whole-language instruction encouraged students to use pictures, context cues, and sentence patterns as substitutes for decoding, producing children who appeared to read but were memorizing or guessing. Janetos is careful to acknowledge what whole-language got right -- authentic literature, vocabulary, writing, and motivation through meaning -- while insisting these goods must be built on top of sound decoding instruction, not substituted for it. The closing argument cites Anita Archer's caution that teachers' science-of-reading training should not overwhelm students with information beyond what accelerates their reading acquisition.
points: Frank Smith's claim that reading is as natural as speaking rests on a category error: biologically primary skills (speaking) are acquired implicitly; biologically secondary skills (reading) require explicit, effortful instruction.

Neuroscience (Dehaene) shows that visual print signals travel to a different brain region than auditory speech, requiring deliberate instruction to create the neural connection -- a connection that does not exist at birth.

Whole-language's three-cueing model (grapho-phonic, syntactic, semantic) misassigned context and pictures to word identification rather than word confirmation, producing children who mimicked reading through memorization.

Alphabetic print is a cultural invention, not a biological adaptation; unlike spoken language, it must be explicitly taught because evolution has not produced mechanisms for acquiring it automatically.

The goal is to get students to decoding escape velocity -- enough understanding to independently enter the world of reading -- without increasing cognitive load by teaching more than is needed for that purpose.
quotes: Once Smith commits to viewing reading as similar to speaking because they are both 'bringing sense to meaningful situations' with 'very little additional effort required to use the eyes,' he straps himself into an instructional straightjacket that prevents acknowledgment of the importance of teaching foundational skills to facilitate access to print.

I am not suggesting that Frank Smith has nothing to say about reading. On the contrary, his emphasis on the importance of meaning-making is significant. I am merely siding with the science when it comes to helping children crack the alphabetic code because there's a reality I cannot alter: my students are wired for sound, not for print.

Alphabetic print is a cultural invention, not a natural biological adaptation. Spoken language arrives already phonologically available to the listener; print does not. Mapping visual symbols onto speech is not merely using the eyes instead of the ears; it requires learning an artificial code.

Context supports comprehension, but it cannot substitute for the development of precise print recognition. Thus, biologically primary skills are acquired implicitly, rapidly, and without formal instruction. By contrast, biologically secondary skills are acquired slowly, effortfully, and typically only through explicit teaching.

What I didn't know when my whole-language colleague and I swapped books -- and what I have only recently discovered -- is David Geary's distinction between biologically primary and biologically secondary knowledge. Since becoming familiar with this distinction, however, I believe it tells me all I need to know about where Smith went wrong in his thinking.
